source.title: Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks
source.authors: Depen Morwani; Benjamin L. Edelman; Costin-Andrei Oncescu; Rosie Zhao; S. Kakade

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analytically characterizes max-margin features and reports training experiments on algebraic tasks, offering a different account and measurements of feature formation than the grokking progress-measure study. It does not test delayed train/test generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses grokking and cites earlier reports of delayed generalization, but those cited results are not recorded as rows. Its own modular-addition results concern maximum-margin solutions, Fourier structure, and normalized-margin trajectories; it does not report training/test accuracy or the removal of memorizing components.
record.test_reason: The paper explains, through max-margin analysis, why one-hidden-layer networks learn Fourier and irreducible-representation features on algebraic tasks. All of its experiments train on the full population dataset (D_p, all of S_n), so there is no held-out test set, no train/test accuracy, and no delayed generalization. It does not track features against any accuracy jump or measure memorizing components, so it cannot show whether progress measures anticipate a transition (V2). It does not compare runs or architectures to see whether they converge to the same algorithm (V6). Grokking appears only as motivation and in cited prior work (Power et al., Nanda et al.). Its results concern which features max-margin solutions have, a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that margin maximization alone can fully specify the features learned in these algebraic tasks (Fourier features for modular addition, irreducible representations for groups, a sign/magnitude structure for sparse parity), analytically explaining Nanda et al. and Chughtai et al. Trained nets approach the predicted margins and features. They also note that the proofs cover only x^2/x^k activations and L2,ν norms, with empirical hints of transfer to other architectures.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies regularized optimization and maximum-margin feature structure in one-hidden-layer networks, including full-population modular addition; it does not reproduce the small train/test split and delayed-accuracy measurement of the original grokking work.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported Fourier concentration differs by activation and regularization: the quadratic network with L2,3 regularization is almost exactly frequency-sparse, whereas the ReLU network with L2 regularization is concentrated around 0.9 but not exactly sparse.

fits_no_version.finding: For quadratic-activation nets, every max-margin solution on full-data modular addition uses single-frequency Fourier neurons covering all frequencies (Theorem 7). Trained nets approach the maximum margin and become nearly exactly 1-sparse (quadratic) or about 0.9-concentrated (ReLU), with frequencies near-uniformly used (Figure 7). Analogous results hold for S3–S5 (irreducible representations) and for sparse parity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Margin maximization (small explicit regularization) alone determines the Fourier/representation-theoretic features networks learn on algebraic tasks. This is a mechanism for why the grokking circuit takes its form, separate from when generalization occurs.

record.problems: The evidence for training dynamics is limited to normalized-margin and feature summaries; the paper reports no train/test accuracy curves or delayed-generalization measurement. Some plotted results are described qualitatively rather than with numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Sparse-parity and finite-group experiments are omitted because the retained rows focus on modular-addition Fourier features and margin progress; those other task results do not measure delayed test-accuracy generalization or its timing.

untested.parts: All: no train/test split, no delayed test-accuracy jump, no training-set-size dependence.
All: no generalization transition, no tracking of memorizing components, no test of whether progress measures anticipate a jump; only final feature structure on full data.
All: no non-algorithmic data, no initialization-scale or weight-norm sweep.
All: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
All: regularization is used to induce margin maximization, but there is no circuit-efficiency comparison, critical dataset size or ungrokking.
No comparison across runs or hyperparameters. The theorem constrains max-margin solutions for x^2 activations with the L2,3 norm only; ReLU is shown only qualitatively, in a single run.
All: no optimizer or floating-point controls.

missing.what: Final distribution of neurons across frequencies is close to uniform for both ReLU and quadratic nets (all frequencies present).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' classification and the V2 labels should be dropped. The experiments use full-population training, so grokking (delayed generalization) cannot occur. The feature result concerns which algorithm the network ends up with, not the gradual-then-sudden dynamics V2 names. A possible V6 reading (max-margin solutions all share Fourier structure) is a theoretical argument limited to quadratic nets and does not compare runs, so no V6 verdict is given. Peer-review venue in the record (ICLR 2023) is not stated in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No small training-set train/test accuracy curves, chance-level test accuracy, delayed test-accuracy rise, or training-set-size comparison.

The paper reports Fourier-feature and normalized-margin results, but does not measure delayed test-accuracy jumps, removal of memorizing components, or whether its progress measures anticipate such a jump.
No non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale or weight-norm transition sweep, or lazy-to-rich comparison.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
No comparison of efficient generalizing circuits with memorization, critical dataset-size prediction, or ungrokking experiment.
No comparison across runs testing whether networks converge to the same algorithm.
No optimizer-instability or floating-point artifact controls.

rows.subject: one-hidden layer network with quadratic activations
rows.operation_detail: Analytically characterizes the maximum L2,3-margin solutions on the full modular-addition dataset.
rows.measure: Maximum-margin feature structure: each neuron uses one frequency, and every frequency ζ ∈ {1, ..., (p−1)/2} is used by at least one neuron.
rows.value: Theorem 7 states that every neuron has Fourier-supported cosine weights at one frequency, and every specified frequency occurs in the network.
rows.note: This is an analytical characterization of max-margin solutions, not a measurement of a delayed generalization transition.
rows.check: This is an analytical theorem (Theorem 7) about max-margin solutions on the full dataset, not a measured result. It says nothing about gradual formation, memorization removal or timing relative to a generalization jump, so it does not bear on V2.

rows.subject: 1-hidden layer quadratic network
rows.operation_detail: Trained with gradient descent and L2,3 regularization; Fourier concentration is reported at the end of training.
rows.measure: Maximum normalized Fourier power of embedding vectors across neurons.
rows.value: The maximum normalized power is almost exactly 1 for all neurons; embeddings are 1-sparse in frequency space.
rows.note: The paper describes the final distribution explicitly; it does not report test accuracy.
rows.check: Final Fourier sparsity of a quadratic net trained on all p^2 pairs, with no test split. It cannot show delayed generalization or whether features anticipate a jump, so it does not bear on V2's dynamics claim.

rows.subject: 1-hidden layer ReLU network
rows.operation_detail: Trained with gradient descent and L2 regularization; Fourier concentration is reported at the end of training.
rows.measure: Maximum normalized Fourier power of embedding vectors across neurons.
rows.value: The final distribution is concentrated around 0.9; neurons are nearly 1-sparse in frequency space but not quite.
rows.note: The paper contrasts this with the quadratic network's near-exact frequency sparsity.
rows.check: Final Fourier concentration (about 0.9) for a ReLU net trained on the full dataset, with no test split. Its 'partial' state was judged against exact 1-sparsity predicted by theory, not against any version, so it does not bear on V2.

rows.subject: 1-hidden layer quadratic network
rows.operation_detail: Reports the normalized L2,3 margin over training.
rows.value: The network asymptotically reaches the maximum L2,3 margin predicted by the analysis.
rows.note: The text describes convergence toward the predicted margin, but gives no test-accuracy jump to compare this progress with.
rows.check: The normalized L2,3 margin trajectory approaches the theoretical maximum. It is not tied to any generalization transition (none exists with full-data training), so it is not a V2 progress measure in the grokking sense.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
